title: FlashAttention explained: attention is slow because of data movement; tile, compute, write back, same answer
summary: FlashAttention doesn't change attention's output; it changes how attention runs on a GPU: split the computation into blocks small enough for on-chip cache, stitch them together with online softmax to get exact results, and never write the N × N matrix to GPU memory. We work through the blockwise softmax by hand, explain why doing more arithmetic makes it faster, and examine the training and long-context experiments.
ai_summary: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness (Dao et al., Stanford University, 2022) argues that attention on GPUs is limited mainly by memory reads and writes, and proposes an IO-aware exact attention algorithm: load Q, K, and V into on-chip SRAM in tiles, merge the tiles with online softmax to get exact results, recompute rather than store the attention matrix during backpropagation, and fuse everything into a single CUDA kernel that provably reduces memory traffic. In experiments, BERT-large training is 15% faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record, GPT-2 end-to-end training is up to 3× faster, and memory grows linearly with sequence length, letting Transformers beat random guessing on Path-X and Path-256 for the first time.
brief: Problem: attention is limited by memory traffic; the standard implementation repeatedly reads and writes the N × N matrix, while approximate attention saves computation but is often not faster.
Method: load tiles into on-chip cache, combine them with online softmax for exact results, recompute instead of storing during backpropagation, and fuse everything into one kernel.
Results: GPT-2 attention is 7.6× faster and end-to-end training up to 3× faster, BERT-large is 15% faster than the MLPerf record, memory grows linearly, and 16K–64K sequences become practical.
Limitations: every attention variant needs hand-written CUDA; only a single GPU is considered; some speedup figures are stated inconsistently.

paper.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
paper.authors: Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, Christopher Ré

cover.headline: FlashAttention in depth
cover.highlight: Slow at data movement, not compute

sections.h: Bottom line: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: In May 2022, Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, and Christopher Ré of Stanford University, along with Atri Rudra of the University at Buffalo, released this paper. It doesn't invent a new kind of attention; the result is **exactly the same** as standard attention. What it changes is *how attention runs on a GPU*.

The starting point is an overlooked fact: on modern GPUs, attention is slow not because there are too many multiplications, but because data is **shuttled back and forth** too much between the GPU's large memory (HBM) and its small on-chip cache (SRAM). The standard implementation writes the whole N × N attention matrix back to device memory, reads it again for softmax, writes it back again, then reads it once more to multiply by V. As sequences grow, this matrix becomes the biggest burden.

FlashAttention's approach is **tiling**: cut Q, K, and V into small pieces, move each into SRAM, compute a full tile of attention on-chip in one go, then use a small trick to stitch the per-tile softmax back into a correct global result. The N × N matrix is never written to device memory. Backpropagation doesn't store it either; instead, it recomputes it on the spot from two saved statistics.

The result: it does slightly more arithmetic, but reads and writes far less memory, so it's faster and uses less memory. The paper's numbers: GPT-2 attention is 7.6× faster; BERT-large training is 15% faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record; GPT-2 end-to-end training is up to 3× faster than the Hugging Face implementation; and memory grows linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically, letting Transformers beat random guessing on the Path-X and Path-256 tasks at 16K and 64K lengths for the first time.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: Attention is bottlenecked by data movement, not arithmetic. Cut the computation into tiles that fit in on-chip cache, compute each tile there before writing it back, and use online softmax to merge the tiles into an exact result: same answer, far less GPU memory traffic.

callout.title: Three small concepts you need
callout.text: Don't worry if they're unfamiliar; these three are enough:
list: **Attention in three steps**: S = QK^{⊺} computes pairwise similarity, P = softmax(S) turns each row into weights that sum to 1, and O = PV produces a weighted sum of values. See our close read on the Transformer for details.

**softmax** turns a row of numbers into probabilities: exponentiate each number, then divide by the sum of all the exponentiated numbers in the row. The catch: to know the row's sum, you need to see the whole row first.
**HBM and SRAM**: GPUs have two main kinds of memory. HBM is the GPU's main memory: large but relatively slow. SRAM is on-chip cache: much faster but very small.

sections.h: The bottleneck is data movement, not compute

blocks.p: The paper uses the A100 as an example: it has 40–80GB of HBM with 1.5–2.0TB/s of bandwidth, and 108 streaming multiprocessors, each with 192KB of SRAM and an estimated ~19TB/s of bandwidth. SRAM is an order of magnitude faster but only totals about 20MB, making it more than a thousand times smaller than HBM.

callout.title: A warehouse and a workbench
callout.text: HBM is the warehouse: it holds everything, but every fetch means a round trip. SRAM is the workbench by your side: grabbing things is instant, but it only holds a few items at a time. The chef (the compute unit) chops extremely fast; the real time sink is running back and forth between the warehouse and the workbench.

blocks.p: The paper splits GPU work into two categories: **compute-bound** operations (large matrix multiplications), whose time depends on how much arithmetic is done, and **memory-bound** operations (elementwise ops, softmax, dropout, normalizations), whose time depends on how much data is read and written. In attention, the two matrix multiplications are separated by softmax, masking, and dropout—memory-bound steps whose inputs and outputs are the large N × N matrix.
The standard implementation (Algorithm 0 in the paper) looks like this:

list: Read Q and K from HBM, compute S = QK^{⊺}, and **write S back to HBM**.
Read S from HBM, compute P = softmax(S), and **write P back to HBM**.
Read P and V from HBM, compute O = PV, and write O back to HBM.

fig.title: As sequence length grows, the attention matrix dominates
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: one attention head with head dimension d = 64. Numbers computed by Lyra-Jade from matrix sizes.
columns: Number of entries in Q, K, V, O (4 × N × d)
Number of entries in S, P (2 × N × N)
How many times larger the latter is (N ÷ 2d)
fig.note: GPT-2's N = 1024 and d = 64 are exactly the second row. The inputs and outputs you actually need all scale with N, but the standard implementation writes and reads the intermediate matrix—which scales with N²—several times.

sections.h: The hard part: softmax needs the whole row, so how do we tile it?

blocks.p: Tiling sounds natural. The hard part is softmax: each weight in a row has to be divided by the sum of the exponentials for the entire row, but a tile only gives you part of the row. The paper uses a known trick, online softmax: with each tile, keep two small numbers, and when later tiles reveal that the previous “maximum” was wrong, rescale past results proportionally.

parts.desc: The maximum seen so far. Subtracting it before exponentiating prevents overflow.
The current sum of exponentials, anchored at m
A correction factor: when the maximum changes, multiply the old sum by this to rebase it.

formula.note: So if you carry just two numbers, (m, ℓ), you can compute softmax tile by tile and end up with exactly the result you would get by seeing the whole row at once. Output O is corrected with the same factors.

fig.title: A hand calculation: two tiles, same result as one pass
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: one row of attention scores [1, 3, 2, 5] with values v = [10, 20, 30, 40], split into two tiles. Numbers computed by Lyra-Jade using the formulas in Section 3.1.
rows: Merge: multiply the tile-1 terms by e^{3−5} = 0.1353 and add.
Reference: seeing the whole row at once
fig.note: The merged output is o = (0.1353 × 1.1353 × 18.81 + 1.0498 × 39.53) ÷ 1.2034 = 36.88, matching a direct calculation. This is what “exact attention” means: not an approximation, only a different order of computation.

blocks.p: Given online softmax, the whole algorithm (Algorithm 1 in the paper) becomes two nested loops:

list: **Outer loop**: split K and V into tiles of size B_{c} and load one tile K_{j}, V_{j} into SRAM at a time.

**Inner loop**: split Q into tiles of size B_{r}, load them into SRAM one by one, compute S_{ij} = Q_{i} K_{j}^{⊺} on-chip along with the row maximums and exponential sums for that tile, then update outputs O_{i} and the statistics (m_{i}, ℓ_{i}) using the correction formulas above and write them back to HBM.
**Tile sizes** are determined by SRAM capacity M: B_{c} ≈ M ÷ 4d, so that these tiles can all fit on-chip at once.
**One kernel**: the matrix multiplication, softmax, masking, dropout, and multiplication by V all happen in the same GPU program, with no intermediate results written out.

blocks.p: **What about backpropagation?** Computing gradients usually requires the two N × N matrices S and P. FlashAttention doesn't store them; it stores only the output O, the per-row (m, ℓ), and the random number generator state needed for dropout. During the backward pass, it recomputes S and P from small tiles of Q, K, and V on-chip. The recomputation repeats some multiplications, but skipping the huge read/write cycle makes the backward pass faster.

callout.title: “Less computation, faster program”
callout.text: Figure 2 of the paper is exactly a counterexample. On GPT-2 medium with sequence length 1024, standard attention performs 66.6 GFLOPs, while FlashAttention rises to 75.2 GFLOPs because of recomputation. Yet memory traffic falls from 40.3GB to 4.4GB, and runtime falls from 41.7ms to 7.3ms. When an operation is memory-bound, moving less data matters more than doing fewer operations.

blocks.p: The paper also analyzes memory traffic (IO complexity) theoretically:

formula.expr: Standard attention: Θ(N d + N^{2}) HBM accesses; FlashAttention: Θ(N^{2} d^{2} / M) HBM accesses

parts.desc: SRAM size. Typical d is 64–128 and M is about 100KB; d² is many times smaller than M, so FlashAttention's access count is many times lower.
The paper also proves that no exact attention algorithm can asymptotically beat this for all values of M.

formula.note: Intuition: each K, V tile can be at most Θ(M) in size, and every tile requires a full pass over Q; larger SRAM means fewer passes.

blocks.p: Many “approximate attention” methods let each token look at only part of the sequence, which should save work in theory but is often not faster in practice because they're also memory-bound. The paper adds a block-level mask to FlashAttention: masked-out blocks are skipped entirely—neither loaded nor computed.

list: Memory traffic is multiplied by a factor s (the fraction of non-zero blocks), and runtime drops proportionally with sparsity.
It's 2–4× faster than FlashAttention itself and can push sequence length to 64K.
On the Long-Range Arena benchmark, it's 2.8× faster than standard attention with comparable accuracy.
Note: this variant is approximate attention; it's no longer “exactly the same as the original”.

fig.title: GPT-2: same model, training time cut by more than half

blocks.p: **Longer context**: the saved time and memory can buy longer sequences. With FlashAttention, GPT-2 small can grow context from 1K to 4K and train in 3.6 days—still about 30% faster than Megatron's 1K version (4.7 days)—while perplexity falls from 18.2 to 17.5.

fig.title: Long-document classification: longer context scores higher (but not always)
fig.subtitle: From Table 5 of the paper: micro-averaged F1, higher is better. Columns are sequence lengths.
rows: ECtHR (European Court of Human Rights cases)
fig.note: On MIMIC, 16K scores 4.3 points above 512; on ECtHR, 8K scores 8.5 points above 512. The “6.4-point gain” in the abstract is the average of these two deltas. MIMIC is actually lower at 1024 and 2048 than at 512, and ECtHR is lower at 16K than at 8K; the paper suggests this may relate to differences in document length distributions.

blocks.p: **Path-X and Path-256**: the task is to decide whether two points are connected in a 128×128 (or 256×256) black-and-white image, which is fed to the model pixel by pixel, yielding sequences of 16K and 64K tokens. Previous Transformers either ran out of memory or could only manage coin-flip-level random guessing. FlashAttention reaches 61.4% on Path-X, and the block-sparse version reaches 63.1% on Path-256.

**Benchmarks**: for typical sequence lengths from 128 to 2K, FlashAttention is up to 3× faster than PyTorch's standard implementation and uses up to 20× less memory, which grows linearly with length. Approximate attention methods begin to overtake it between 512 and 1024, while the block-sparse version is faster than all known implementations at every length. Compared with Apex FMHA, which was specially optimized for short sequences at the time, it's about 4% slower at length 128 and 8% and 5% faster at 256 and 512.

sections.h: Limitations, and a few details worth noting

blocks.p: The paper lists these limitations:

list: **Hand-written CUDA**: each new attention variant needs a new low-level kernel, which is a lot of engineering and may not transfer directly to other GPU architectures. The paper hopes such implementations can eventually be compiled automatically from high-level languages like PyTorch.
**Single GPU only**: data transfer between multiple GPUs is another layer of IO, which the paper doesn't address.

blocks.p: A few things we noticed while reading the paper:

list: **Inconsistent speedup vs. Megatron**: the start of Section 4 says GPT-2 is 1.8× faster than Megatron, while the Table 2 notes and main text say 1.7×. Working from Table 2's days, small gives 4.7 ÷ 2.7 ≈ 1.7 and medium gives 11.5 ÷ 6.9 ≈ 1.7.

**The “up to 3×” claim is lower than the table shows**: the abstract and the Table 2 notes both say it is up to 3× faster than the Hugging Face implementation, but the GPT-2 small row in Table 2 lists 3.5× (9.5 days vs. 2.7 days).

**Path-X's 61.4% owes something to extra fine-tuning**: the appendix notes that the best Path-X checkpoint was fine-tuned for another 200 epochs, which added about 4 percentage points for FlashAttention.
**The “6.4-point gain” is an average**: the two datasets are 4.3 and 8.5 points respectively, and the scores do not rise monotonically with length (see the table above).
**A subscript typo in Algorithm 1**: line 4 writes the output tiles as O_{i}, ..., O_{T_{r}}, but the first should be O_{1}; the ℓ tiles have the same issue.

sections.h: Afterward: almost the default attention implementation

list: **FlashAttention-2 and -3**: the authors later kept improving parallelism and hardware-specific optimizations for newer GPUs, further increasing speed.

**Adopted into mainstream frameworks**: this kind of tiled, fused, never-materialized attention implementation was later widely adopted by mainstream training and inference frameworks; in many cases, users get it without changing any code.

**A foundation for long context**: memory growing linearly with length is one of the engineering prerequisites that later made it possible to scale context from thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens; combined with the RoPE extrapolation method covered in the previous article, long contexts became truly usable.

**The IO-aware mindset**: the paper's emphasis on “figure out how data moves first” influenced much later inference-optimization work, including PagedAttention in this site's reading list, which manages the KV cache.

**Same author, another path**: lead author Tri Dao later became one of the authors of Mamba, a paper that sidesteps attention's quadratic complexity by changing the architecture; it is the 11th article in this series.

blocks.p: Next up: another inference bottleneck—**GQA, grouped-query attention**. It lets multiple attention heads share one set of keys and values, shrinking the KV cache that inference reads over and over.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: How does the attention result computed by FlashAttention compare with standard attention?
options: It is an approximate result, with very small error.
It is exactly the same; only the order of computation and the way GPU memory is read and written differ.
More accurate, because it uses higher precision.
It is identical only for short sequences.
quiz.why: FlashAttention is exact attention: after tiling plus online softmax correction, it is mathematically identical to computing attention in one pass. Only the block-sparse variant is approximate.

quiz.q: FlashAttention does slightly more computation than standard attention—why is it faster?
options: Because attention is memory-bound: it keeps the N × N matrix in on-chip cache, reducing GPU memory traffic by about 9×.
quiz.why: Figure 2 of the paper: GFLOPs rise from 66.6 to 75.2, but memory traffic falls from 40.3GB to 4.4GB and runtime falls from 41.7ms to 7.3ms.

quiz.q: When computing softmax in tiles, why do you need to keep track of each row's maximum m and exponential sum ℓ?
options: Because later tiles may contain larger values, and you need these two numbers to rescale previous partial results proportionally.
To randomly drop part of the attention.
quiz.why: The softmax denominator is the sum of exponentials for the whole row. As long as you keep (m, ℓ), when a new tile arrives you multiply the old result by e^{old m - new m} to correct it, and the final result is exactly the same as seeing the whole row at once.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: Why is attention said to be bottlenecked by “data movement” rather than “compute”? What is the difference between HBM and SRAM?
Which large matrices does standard attention write to GPU memory, and why do they grow quadratically with sequence length?
How does online softmax stitch tiled results into an exact result?
During backpropagation, why does FlashAttention choose recomputation over storing the attention matrix?
Among the paper's speedup numbers, which refer to end-to-end training and which refer only to attention itself?
